assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock is the cleanest case on the list of a new measurement method that changed what can be measured. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removes the lattice light shift while atoms are confined in the Lamb-Dicke regime, giving many atoms and very narrow linewidths at once. Ye's group then pushed it to the 1e-18 level and below, with clock comparisons that enable relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and dark-matter searches, and a path to redefining the second. Originality, clarity and breadth of impact are all high.
assessment.attribution: Katori (magic-wavelength lattice concept, first realization) and Ye (systematic demonstration of record accuracy and stability, spectroscopy and many-body clock work) are the two decisive names and form a natural two-person share. Credit for the underlying ideas of trapping ions and atoms and of frequency combs has already been recognized in earlier prizes, which helps keep this award focused.
assessment.maturity: Strong and independent confirmation from many labs (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, others) and several species (Sr, Yb, Hg). Redefinition of the second is still pending, but the technique is well established and recognition would be timely.
uncertainties: Which of Katori and Ye the committee views as the primary originator versus the main developer could be debated, and other groups (for example the Sr/Yb/Hg clock community) may be seen as contributors.
I am relying on memory for the clock-comparison record values and have not verified them here.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms turned the interference of massive particles into an instrument. Light-pulse atom interferometers give gravimeters, gyroscopes, measurements of the fine-structure constant and G, and tests of the equivalence principle, with sensitivity scaling that is now competitive with or better than classical devices. This is exactly the kind of method that opens new observations, and it is also being developed for gravity sensing in geoscience and navigation.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard (first atom interferometers with material gratings and light, including early work with MIT), Kasevich and Chu (the Stanford light-pulse gravimeter and gyroscope) and Borde (theory of Ramsey-Borde interferometers) all contributed; Chu received a prize in 1997 for cooling, which complicates a fair configuration. The three listed names are a defensible set but Chu's role is not in the credited names and I cannot add it.
assessment.maturity: More than three decades of experimental confirmation and commercial and field deployments. Large-scale gravitational-wave and dark-matter-oriented atom interferometers are still developing but the core technique is mature.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 1997 cooling prize and credit priority among Pritchard, Kasevich, Borde and others who are not credited here.
Not all state-of-the-art claims (for example sensitivity records) have been independently checked by me.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Spherical-aberration correction broke a limit that Scherzer showed in 1936 and brought sub-angstrom, atomic-resolution imaging to routine electron microscopy. It is a quintessential instrumentation advance: a new capability to see structure, interfaces and defects, with huge reach across physics, materials science and chemistry. Its impact is broad and measurable, and the clear experimental demonstration is precisely what I prefer.
assessment.attribution: Rose (the theoretical design of the corrector), Haider (building and demonstrating the first working corrector in TEM) and Urban (STEM/TEM application and the Julich collaboration) are the natural trio; Krivanek's STEM corrector is a competing contribution that is not among the credited names, which makes the attribution contested.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature: widely deployed for two decades with multiple independent implementations and many downstream discoveries.
uncertainties: Competing credit for Krivanek and colleagues in STEM correction is outside the credited names.
Whether the committee regards this as physics or chemistry or materials instrumentation, given that the 1986 Ruska prize and the 2017 chemistry cryo-EM prize already covered adjacent areas.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light for interferometry connects a quantum-optics idea to a real measurement gain: Caves's 1981 proposal for beating the standard quantum limit in interferometers, the first experimental squeezing demonstrations, and the routine use of squeezed vacuum in GEO600 and LIGO/Virgo to improve sensitivity to gravitational waves. It is a clear example of quantum resources improving a real instrument.
assessment.attribution: Caves is the theorist who proposed the application; Kimble's group produced early squeezing by four-wave mixing and cavity work (Slusher and others at Bell Labs observed first squeezing, which is not credited); Schnabel led the implementation in GEO600 and later detectors. The credited names are plausible but several other experimentalists have claims.
assessment.maturity: Squeezing is now operating in observatories and is independently confirmed; the application is mature, though the underlying 2017 gravitational-wave prize already recognized the detectors.
uncertainties: Priority of the first squeezing observation (Slusher et al.) and the many contributors to detector squeezing are not covered by the credited names.
Overlap with the 2017 LIGO prize may weigh against.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cirac and Zoller's 1995 proposal and the subsequent experimental demonstrations of gates, entanglement and error-corrected operations in trapped ions established a leading platform for quantum computation and quantum simulation. The field has produced the most precise quantum logic gates and long coherence times, matters I value as an experimentalist.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller are the theorists; Blatt is the leading experimentalist for gates, entanglement of many ions and quantum algorithms. Wineland and Monroe's work (Wineland was recognized in 2012 for measurement and manipulation of single quantum systems) is substantial and Monroe is not in the credited names.
assessment.maturity: The first gate demonstrations are three decades old and have been widely reproduced. Scalable machines are still developing, so impact beyond physics is not yet realized.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 Wineland prize and the omission of Monroe, Wineland and others from the credited names.
Premature if the committee wants proof of practical computation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realized strongly correlated lattice models, including the observation of the superfluid to Mott-insulator transition and, later, single-site-resolved quantum gas microscopy. These are controllable quantum simulators with direct imaging of many-body states, opening new ways to observe quantum matter.
assessment.attribution: Zoller and Jaksch proposed the Hubbard-model mapping; Greiner and Bloch (with Hansch) did the 2002 Mott transition, and Greiner and Bloch both developed quantum gas microscopes. The credited trio is natural, though Jaksch and Hansch are left out, and the BEC prize of 2001 overlaps in the background.
assessment.maturity: Mature and widely reproduced, with a broad community and a continuing flow of results, although practical applications remain mostly scientific.
uncertainties: Credit split between theory (Zoller, Jaksch) and experiment (Bloch, Greiner, others such as Esslinger or Gross) is not unique.
Overlap with candidate B035 and with the Rydberg and trapped-ion platforms.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single nitrogen-vacancy spins in diamond gave a room-temperature solid-state qubit and a nanoscale sensor for magnetic fields, temperature and electric fields, with applications in biology and materials. Quantum sensing is the practical link to measurement that I find compelling.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko demonstrated single-NV optical detection and coherent control in 1997 and the early 2000s; Lukin contributed to quantum registers, sensing and theory. Credit is shared with Awschalom, Hanson, Yacoby, Budker and others.
assessment.maturity: Independently confirmed by many groups; sensing applications are growing quickly but the field is still maturing and the most striking applications are recent.
uncertainties: Large number of strong contributors outside the credited names, and Lukin appears on several candidates.
Whether the discovery is best framed as a qubit or a sensor.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical coherence tomography is a measurement technique with enormous reach beyond physics: micrometer-scale depth-resolved imaging, now standard in ophthalmology and cardiology. The physics is low-coherence interferometry, a clear instrument invention with decisive societal impact.
assessment.attribution: The 1991 Science paper credits Huang, Swanson, Fujimoto and colleagues, including Puliafito, Schuman and Izatt; Fercher's earlier low-coherence interferometry for eye measurements is also relevant. A fair configuration among the three credited names is possible but contested.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature, with decades of clinical use and independent developments such as Fourier-domain and swept-source OCT.
uncertainties: Whether the committee views this as physics rather than medicine or engineering.
Priority of Fercher and others, and the many parties who made OCT clinical, who are not among the credited names.
